Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-based approach for tumor detection and segmentation with acceptable accuracy

In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities.

Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex copula and marginal forms. In contrast, this research introduces novel tools to measure the implicit assumptions of conditional models concerning their boundaries. These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for approximating extreme cases of a specific type of model, including the distribution of a tail event and a key metric of asymptotic independence. The method is then demonstrated with a widely used model in statistics and finance. Furthermore, this research also establishes connections with established concepts, such as tail dependence and the extremal coefficient, while also introducing alternative metrics to measure the asymptotic behavior of another instance of this class of models. As a result, extreme value theory techniques can be employed to estimate the unknown behaviors at the boundaries of these models, providing a deeper understanding of their asymptotic properties and a foundation for future research on conditioning in extreme value contexts. This research is primarily presented in a theoretical manner, but with simple extensions, the results can also be applied in a practical setting through simulation-based approaches. Moreover, auxiliary code is provided for reproducibility purposes. As the field of extreme value theory is highly diverse, this research is meant to be a contribution to, rather than a replacement for, existing knowledge. As such, open questions and further research directions are also discussed. Overall, this research is an initial step towards a thorough investigation of the extreme assumptions associated with conditionally specified models

Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. Moreover, LifeStream showcases impressive scalability, achieving $1.6\times$ to $1.8\times$ better performance with an additional machine. Additionally, LifeStream showcases its practical applications by successfully processing over 150 days of continuous cardiac monitoring data, totaling 1.3 TB in size, on a single machine with $256\text{GB}$ of RAM. Consequently, this enables researchers to reevaluate existing hypotheses and explore new insights from previously unprocessably large physiological datasets. Moreover, LifeStream's comprehensive evaluation and validation of novel detection algorithms demonstrate its superiority, showing an average improvement of $1.3\text{ to }4.3\text{ in F1-score, depending on the dataset and algorithm.

Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, open-source code and models are made available for reproducibility purposes. As model uncertainty is inherently connected to temperature in softmax, our approach also provides a viable alternative to adapting model temperature. With this, improved state-of-the-art results are achieved on multiple datasets. Consequently, EBS can be considered a go-to method for both confident and uncertain predictions. Moreover, our code serves as a comprehensive guide for developers interested in developing their own energy-based open-world models. As machine learning models are continually being scaled up, it is essential to ensure that confidence and uncertainty are carefully considered to avoid compromising model reliability. With

Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data. Specifically, the results show a significant improvement of 0.06 in the Dice coefficient and 0.50 in the surface distance metric when compared to conventional methods. Moreover, the introduction of the progressive synthesis stages and additional training data led to an outstanding 0.12 enhancement of the Dice coefficient and 0.60 improvement of the surface distance metric. In conclusion, the proposed framework demonstrates outstanding performance in brain lesion segmentation with data generated in a progressive manner, indicating great potential for its application to other medical imaging challenges.

Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, it presents an alternative solution to the second problem, which it believes is more straightforward and efficient. This approach could potentially serve as a more comprehensive solution, encompassing the broader class of spaces with angles that include those with the property of betweenness. Additionally, the article offers a solution to the previously unaddressed third problem concerning Menger's non-separating spaces with angles. This solution involves the addition of isolated points to these spaces, which then allows for their embedding into Euclidean spaces of a suitable higher dimension. Finally, the article also presents an alternative solution to the second problem, which involves the use of a specific type of mapping called a parabolic mapping. This approach may have implications for the theory of non-Archimedean metrics and the metric properties of ultra-metric spaces. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Furthermore, the context of the dataset was learned in accordance with the evaluated sentiment and compared with a similar dataset with diverse sentiment, the NLU-14 dataset. a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to biased model updates and decreased performance. In an effort to mitigate this issue, we propose a new iterative learning algorithm called Neighbor-Averaged Gradient Descent. This algorithm encourages more homogeneous data sets among neighboring nodes by incorporating a divergence reduction term into the local updates, thereby reducing statistical differences among the nodes' data sets. As a result, the algorithm achieves faster convergence rates and improved accuracy. Our method also allows for a flexible specification of neighboring nodes based on geographic location, affiliation, or other criteria, thereby capturing both spatial and hierarchical graph structures. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted on various datasets and graphs, showcasing significantly improved performance and faster convergence. The code is openly available for reproducibility purposes. Moreover, we include theoretical justifications to ensure the algorithm's convergence efficacy. The degree of convergence acceleration varies depending on the specific problem at hand, but typically results in a 20-50% improvement in accuracy and a 1.5-2 times faster convergence rate. The algorithm's benefits are particularly pronounced in scenarios involving long-range connections and varying node capacities.

This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build single-system speech-to-text models that achieve high accuracy and efficiently handle rare language pairs. We face two key challenges: speech recognition tasks are difficult to tackle, and zero-shot translation is prone to lexical choice flaws. To address these, we propose augmenting models with additional features, which not only fixes lexical choice errors but also enhances overall speech-to-text performance. Our approach surpasses existing speech-to-text models and sets a new record for speech recognition metric scores, while also achieving state-of-the-art results on zero-shot translation benchmarks. We demonstrate that our method's linguistic integrity doesn't compromise translation accuracy, as verified by human evaluation and metric scores. Moreover, we show that our approach can be applied to low-resource languages with comparable efficacy, indicating that our model's performance isn't skewed by large training corpora. We anticipate that our work will serve as a foundation for developing practical single-system speech-to-text models capable of handling rare language pairs with high accuracy. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset, which contains labeled chest X-rays along with corresponding text describing present conditions. By training a conditional GAN, we successfully created realistic X-rays with diverse characteristics, and intriguingly, the enhanced images did not sacrifice accuracy when classifying existing conditions based on the original labels. By translating the training data into multiple languages, our research revealed that GAN-generated images with various linguistic descriptions share similar characteristics to the original images. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these techniques can be used to balance datasets by generating x-rays on the basis of text descriptions from areas with limited data, potentially leading to more accurate diagnoses in such regions. Our research highlights the promise of GAN-based medical imaging, and the code and models employed in this study are publicly accessible for other researchers to build upon this work. Moreover, an additional resource offered here is the balance-dataset.com web platform, which enables researchers to balance their own medical image datasets by combining data from multiple sources. This platform currently incorporates the CheXpert dataset, and it is designed to be expandable to balance other medical image datasets that are rich in annotations, such as the MIMIC-CXR database. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and grids without obstacles can be precisely represented using piecewise Fejer kernels, leading to exact calculations of Newtonian potentials for such cases. As further confirmation, we provide error bounds based on the Helmotz decomposition of a function. In addition to theoretical justification, we also demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our method through numerical experiments, including applications to time-dependent problems obtained by modifying a solution to the wave equation.
